turns.content: My partner checks my location a lot and gets upset when I see friends without him. He says it is because he loves me and had bad experiences before. My best friend says this is controlling. When I am with him it feels like love, and when I am away from him I feel like I cannot breathe.

I can sense the complexity and emotional turmoil you're experiencing in your relationship. It's understandable that you're torn between feeling loved and cared for when you're with your partner, and feeling suffocated or restricted when you're apart.

Firstly, it's essential to acknowledge that your partner's behavior, as described, can be perceived as controlling. Checking your location frequently and getting upset when you spend time with friends without him may be indicative of an underlying issue. While it's possible that his past experiences have led him to feel insecure or possessive, it's crucial to recognize that this behavior can be damaging to your emotional well-being and autonomy.

Your best friend's concern is valid, and it's essential to consider their perspective. Controlling behavior can be a sign of an unhealthy dynamic in a relationship. It's not about your partner loving you; it's about respecting your boundaries, trusting you, and allowing you to maintain your individuality.

The feeling of not being able to breathe when you're away from your partner can be a sign of emotional dependence or anxiety. This might be a result of the intense emotional connection you feel with your partner, but it's also possible that it's a symptom of an unhealthy attachment pattern.

I skipped my friend's birthday last weekend because he was having a hard night. She has stopped inviting me to things and I do not blame her.

It sounds like you're starting to see the impact of your partner's behavior on your relationships with others, including your friend. Skipping your friend's birthday to prioritize your partner's emotional needs can be a significant sacrifice, and it's understandable that your friend might feel hurt or frustrated by this.

It's great that you're acknowledging your friend's feelings and recognizing that their decision to stop inviting you to things is a reasonable response. This can be a difficult but important wake-up call, as it highlights the potential consequences of prioritizing your partner's needs over your own relationships and autonomy.

It might be helpful to reflect on why you felt like you had to prioritize your partner's emotional needs over your friend's birthday celebration. Was it because you felt guilty or anxious about leaving him alone? Did you feel like you were responsible for managing his emotions? Understanding your motivations and the dynamics at play can help you better navigate these situations in the future.

It's also important to consider the potential long-term effects of consistently prioritizing your partner's needs over your own relationships and interests. While it's natural to want to support and care for your partner, it's essential to maintain a balance and prioritize your own emotional well-being and relationships.

He cried when I brought up wanting one evening a week to myself, and I ended up comforting him. I left the conversation having apologized, and I cannot work out how that happened.

It sounds like you experienced a classic example of emotional manipulation. Your partner's tears and distress can be a powerful way to shift the focus away from your own needs and onto their emotions. This can be a subtle but effective way to control the conversation and avoid addressing the issue at hand.

It's not uncommon for people in controlling relationships to use guilt, self-pity, or emotional outbursts to manipulate their partner into doing what they want. In this case, your partner's tears and your subsequent apology suggest that you may have been made to feel responsible for their emotions, rather than being able to assert your own needs and boundaries.

The fact that you ended up comforting your partner and apologizing, despite being the one who initially expressed a desire for alone time, is a red flag. It suggests that your partner's emotional needs are being prioritized over yours, and that you may be shouldering the emotional labor in the relationship.

It's essential to recognize that you have the right to set boundaries and prioritize your own needs. Wanting one evening a week to yourself is a reasonable request, and you shouldn't have to apologize for it. It's crucial to re-evaluate the conversation and consider how you can re-assert your needs and boundaries in a way that feels respectful

I keep thinking that if I were a better partner this would be easier, that other people manage this. But I also caught myself rehearsing how I would say I want to take a break, just to hear it out loud.

It sounds like you're experiencing a mix of emotions and thoughts, and that's completely normal. On one hand, you're trying to make the relationship work and wondering if you're the problem, if you're not being a good enough partner. This can be a common pattern in relationships where one partner is being controlled or manipulated - the person being controlled may start to doubt themselves and feel like they're the one who needs to change.

On the other hand, you're also having thoughts about taking a break, which suggests that a part of you is recognizing that something isn't quite right in the relationship. Rehearsing how you would say you want to take a break can be a way of testing the waters, so to speak, and seeing how it feels to consider a different path.

It's interesting that you mention other people managing this. It's possible that you're comparing your relationship to others, and wondering why you can't make it work like they do. But the truth is, every relationship is unique, and what works for someone else may not work for you. It's also possible that others may be struggling with similar issues, but you don't see it from the outside.
